how: Calls recruit members to draw the shared mark, add familiar emblems, and coordinate a timed expansion.
A participant explicitly judges the rainbow to have too many people and calls for moving upward.
The reply to the drawing call reports partial completion, supporting a call-to-building sequence without identifying every participant's motive.
Judging the rainbow stronger is given as the reason to move upward.
The member who asks for help supplies a project that another member subsequently reports partly completed.
Members propose, enlarge, sign, and add familiar figures to a changing cluster rather than settling one final design once.
Members report the Nail and Gear present and Brady being built, providing states of work rather than verified placement logs.
A request for a visible grid receives a hand-done grid, while coordinates locate another proposed gathering point.
A member adapts a drawing script, while other participants object that scripts spoil enjoyment and collaboration.
Automatic drawing must track revised plans because participants attribute new vandalism to scripts left running.
An apparent unlimited-placement glitch supplies extra placements without evidence of scripts, spare accounts, or a deliberate machine workaround.
The room supplies a local exception to undecided order through explicit design votes, without testing the model's population frequency.
The initiating proposal and recruitment are fused in one call, so a separate starter-to-call sequence cannot be inferred.
A requested grid refines an existing template, so template circulation can continue after a design artifact already exists.
The record supports requesting and supplying a grid but does not establish that a template settled the room's design disagreement.
A participant answers the report of carrying a proposal with a brief thank-you that requests nothing in return.
The brief thank-you answers a relay report rather than a placement call, leaving the proposed call-acceptance mechanism untested.
Participants rally under attack, protect the logo, shift from finishing to upkeep, and hand maintenance to others while resting.
One passage explicitly moves from declaring the work completed to asking that it be kept clean.
Upkeep precedes script sharing, but the coded script announcement does not attribute adoption to insufficient hands or attack pressure.
Participants diagnose automatic placement as the source of vandalism, and a user acknowledges the script in an apology.
A participant proposes moving after the rainbow erases the drawing, and another calls for moving because the rainbow has more people.
Members offer mutual non-destruction, redesign to spare neighbours, and bargain over sacrificing a flag while keeping a face.
Participants revise the plan to preserve neighbouring art and offer to stop overwrites and help repair damage.
Members seek protection, offer restoration, thank a proposal carrier, and report helping another community.
A member reports carrying a border proposal to another room's sticky, while another describes playing diplomat.
The opposing parties can be factions inside the same community, so negotiated coexistence cannot require separate rooms.
Repair offers and restraint remain individual commitments while later complaints report renewed overwriting, leaving collective compliance unresolved.
Border talk also addresses damage caused by the room's own expansion, rather than only neighbours eroding its work.
A plan to preserve neighbouring art and later repair offers do not establish that a settled boundary produced sustained restraint.
A proposed trade over flag and face receives a promise to try preserving the face, demonstrating negotiated help rather than completed pixel protection.
Protection requests and reported help are visible, but the record does not establish a shortage-driven request followed by fulfilled outside help.
Alliance promotion and reported diplomacy do not establish whether this room joined a functioning coalition.
The record cannot establish that upkeep pressure led to coalition membership or joint defence.
Reported presence in the Grey Blob does not establish a host ruling on permission or governing the guest work.
Individual bargains and attempts to stop others are visible without an explicit dispute over who may bind the room.
Negotiation is observed but no coded response disputes a negotiator's mandate, so the proposed authority-dispute mechanism remains unresolved.
Existing rebel and loyalist identities enter calls, competitive comparisons, and admitted vandalism inside the community.
Members act through familiar flag lore while still recognising rival supporters as their own people.
Participants turn visible damage into a pop-culture likeness rather than only repairing or mourning it.
Participants use canvas outcomes to test familiar claims about flag love and challenge the inference with differences in how easily flags scale.
Inherited rivalry names targets within one room, and solidarity with those targets also appears, so rivalry does not imply a stable external enemy.
A member proposes one coordination thread to prevent spam and another proposes a dedicated organising subreddit.
The request for a coordination thread explicitly links concentrating canvas posts to avoiding a flood, without proving moderator adoption.
Flag lore and pixel rebellion do not themselves demonstrate an April Fools takeover or deceptive host framing.
Members celebrate collective achievement, claim hours of labour, and reflect on enjoying work together.
Participants mark closure and mourn an imperfect finish, while another post preserves the corner's birth in a timelapse.
Members propose episode artwork and advertise replacement canvases, without establishing that proposals became lasting collective arrangements.
A single passage combines completion, thanks to contributors, and a handoff to keeping the work clean.
Celebration and later recording coexist, but no coded passage establishes that celebration prompted the timelapse or memorial record.
Episode-art reuse is proposed, but replacement-canvas announcements do not establish that preserving a record caused continued pixel-making.
A cleanup claim and proposed episode art do not establish disagreement about which version should be preserved.
The canvas brings a visitor into the room, where the visitor asks what the community is because its sidebar does not explain it.
One participant admits vandalising the Nail and Gear and another proposes placing Brady over the rival flag.
Competitive flag taunts and objections concern factions within the room, so carrying a contest in talk must allow internal rivals.
Recruitment and later vandalism are visible, but the concepts do not establish that recruitment caused the attack.
Attack, apology, and restraint are visible without a coded direct refusal of an attack call that establishes the proposed response mechanism.
Internal truces and attack admissions are visible, but their order and motivating connection cannot be established from the coded turns.
Taunting and admitted vandalism occur without evidence that an attack first created the named rival.
